claims.text: Controlled processing such as HIP with slow cooling forms uniformly dispersed, fine secondary HCP precipitates in the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating.
The secondary HCP precipitates impede dislocation climb.
Inhibiting dislocation climb with HCP precipitates enhances creep resistance under sustained loading.
Conventional processing can leave the coating as a supercooled single-phase BCC or FCC matrix.
Conventional processing can produce an inhomogeneous precipitate distribution with coarse precipitates at grain boundaries.
HIP with slow cooling promotes formation and uniform dispersion of a secondary HCP phase in the matrix.
The relevant operating regime is sustained high-temperature loading in which creep dominates plastic deformation.
The HCP precipitates are likely enriched in Zr and Hf.
Evenly distributed HCP precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
HCP precipitates increase the effective activation energy for creep.
Precipitation strengthening limits progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
A HIP-processed coating with uniformly dispersed HCP precipitates will have a lower creep strain rate than a coating with grain-boundary-concentrated precipitates.
A HIP-processed coating will have higher microhardness than the starting baseline.
An inhomogeneous or single-phase baseline has higher dislocation mobility and faster creep deformation.
The proposed strengthening mechanism operates when dislocation climb is the rate-controlling creep process.
The proposed mechanism ceases to govern once dynamic recrystallization or diffusional creep becomes dominant.
